title: From Confusion to Clarity: Creating Common Expectations for AI Use
author: Jennifer W. Shewmaker and Julie Crum
summary: Jennifer Shewmaker and Julie Crum identify the hidden cost of inconsistent AI expectations in schools: the cognitive load imposed on students who must re-decode each teacher's unstated rules every time they change classrooms. They argue that the leadership question has moved beyond whether AI belongs in education to how schools can provide enough structural consistency that students feel confident while preserving teachers' professional flexibility. Drawing on their experience at Lipscomb University, they emphasize that clarity is a support for learning rather than a constraint on it, and that students should understand AI expectations before an assignment—not discover the boundary by accidentally crossing it.
points: The problem is not that teachers hold different AI expectations—that is pedagogically appropriate—but that students bear the full cognitive burden of decoding unstated, inconsistent rules across subjects.
Students spend mental energy guessing 'Am I allowed to use AI for this?' rather than investing that energy in learning—a systemic inefficiency that well-designed leadership can eliminate.
The current leadership question is not whether AI belongs in education but how to create enough structural consistency that students feel safe while preserving teacher professional discretion.
The principle at Lipscomb: clarity supports learning; expectations should be explicit before an assignment begins, not discovered by students through unintentional violations.
Policies alone do not translate into clear expectations on an ordinary Monday morning; the gap between policy and practice is the specific leadership problem schools need to solve.
quotes: The challenge isn't that teachers approach AI differently but that students are left trying to decode a brand-new set of rules every time they change classes.

Students aren't always asking, 'How do I do this assignment?' More often they're wondering, 'Am I allowed to use AI for this? If so, how can I use it?' That's mental energy we want them investing in learning, not in guessing about expectations.

The real leadership challenge of the AI era—providing enough structure for both teachers and students so there is clarity rather than fear while allowing room for the flexibility needed for different fields, levels of learning, and learning outcomes.
Policies alone, however, don't always translate into clear expectations on an ordinary weekday morning. Too often, students discover the boundaries only after they've crossed them.

A principle we've been emphasizing at Lipscomb is that clarity supports learning. The important thing is that students understand the expectations before they begin an assignment, not after they've unintentionally crossed a line.
